doc.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Double bass drums and the great drummers
title: Ambidextrous ideas: extra snares and the silent practice kit
summary: He recalls other drum inventions, including a rubber practice set he could not patent.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: You said you did it in a class. Was it shop class, art class, design class? Why were you drawing this, and why did your teacher approve it? Was it a music teacher?

I knew I was really ambidextrous. I started dreaming about this idea of having another drum on this side. Later on I was the first one to have two snare drums over here and then have an extension of bongo drums over here. So those ideas were coming to me. I was the first one that invented the silent drum set. I had a practice pad with rubber on the top, and then cymbals made out of rubber. That was the silent drum set. I could practice in the dressing room without bothering anybody. Then later on guys came out with a sophisticated practice set. But I couldn’t get those things – what do you call it? – invented – patent. I couldn’t get a patent on it, because I didn’t know what I was doing. I was a kid. I showed somebody the idea. They’d steal it from me.

We’re going to talk about your relationship with Remo Belli later, so we can talk about how you were able to develop a lot of – and work with somebody who’s developing the instrument. Again, that’s one of the other things that makes Louie Bellson’s history so important, because you have all these other activities as well as being a drummer. At this point let’s take a break.
